findings.headline: Disabled Facilities Grants spend was £187,912 against a £400,000 budget to 30 September 2026, with a delay in invoicing for the second quarter.
findings.detail: Applications are processed by Portsmouth City Council on Fareham's behalf, with some small house clearance works managed in-house. The paper names the invoicing delay as the reason the spend is low against the profiled budget.
findings.matters: Delegated processing through a neighbouring council means invoicing timing can hold back reported capital spend, which affects shared-service arrangements elsewhere.
findings.figures: £1,310,200 scheme budget; £400,000 budget to 30 Sep 26; £187,912 actual to 30 Sep 26
findings.quote: There has been a delay in invoicing for the second

findings.headline: The National Lottery Heritage Fund has approved the continuation of Holly Hill Rediscovered and the requested budget uplift.
findings.detail: The project is progressing to RIBA Stage 4 (Construction) after the Landscape Architect was reappointed. The paper says the Fund continues to commend the way the Council is managing and delivering the project.
findings.matters: External grant funder approval of a budget uplift is the kind of outcome other councils running heritage-funded schemes will want to know about.
findings.figures: £2,044,803 scheme budget; £358,800 added to scheme budget in February 2026
findings.quote: The National Lottery Heritage Fund (NLHF) has approved both the continuation of the project and the requested budget uplift.

findings.headline: The fair value of the Council's 10 commercial investment properties fell by £1,605,000 since 2025, with five properties rising in value and five falling.
findings.detail: The overall property portfolio, including the commercial properties, fell by £1,862,000 over the same period. The paper describes fluctuations as market sentiment rather than actual gains or losses. Contracted income is estimated at £4.1 million in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Falls in commercial property fair value affect the income and asset position of any council with a commercial property portfolio, and lenders track this exposure.
findings.figures: £1,605,000 decrease in fair value; £1,862,000 overall portfolio decrease; £33,825k value at 31 March 2025 to £32,220k at 31 March 2026; £4.1 million contracted income 2026/27
findings.quote: Since 2025 the Fair Value of the portfolio has decreased by £1,605,000.

findings.headline: Treasury management investments earned a net rate of return of 1.4% to 30 September 2026, against a 2.9% estimate, while commercial investments earned 4.4% against 3.6%.
findings.detail: The rate of return indicator is net of associated costs and shows the half-year position. The paper does not give a reason for the difference from the estimate.
findings.matters: A treasury return running below estimate at the half-year point is a figure finance directors will check against their own investment income forecasts.
findings.figures: Treasury management investments: 2.9% estimate, 1.4% actual to 30 Sept; Commercial investments: 3.6% estimate, 4.4% actual to 30 Sept; Total: 3.4% estimate, 3.5% actual
findings.quote: Treasury Management Investments 2.9% 1.4%

findings.headline: £12 million invested in strategic pooled funds returned an average total return of 5.10% to 30 September 2026, comprising a 4.49% income return.
findings.detail: The paper says the income return is used to support services in year. It adds 0.62% of unrealised capital gains. The investment table shows a pooled fund balance of £10,913k, and Appendix B refers to £11 million.
findings.matters: A council drawing a 4.49% income return from strategic funds to support services is a choice that other councils with similar investments will compare against cash returns.
findings.figures: £12 million in pooled funds (para 26); £10,913k balance at 30 Sept 2026; 5.10% average total return; 4.49% income return; 0.62% unrealised capital gains; £11 million (Appendix B)
findings.quote: These funds generated an average total return of 5.10%, comprising a 4.49% income return

findings.headline: Bank Rate has held at 3.75% since December 2025, while markets now anticipate a higher Bank Rate after September inflation forecasts.
findings.detail: Arlingclose expects Bank Rate to stay at 3.75%, but the paper says upside risks have increased due to higher energy prices and uncertainty about the Government's forthcoming Budget.
findings.matters: A treasury adviser's view that rates will hold while markets price in a rise is the assumption set that councils and lenders will be pricing against.
findings.figures: 3.75% Bank Rate since December 2025
findings.quote: have led markets to anticipate a higher Bank Rate.

findings.headline: General Fund net interest was £380,928 at the end of September 2026 against a £468,400 budget for the year, compared with £277,140 a year earlier.
findings.detail: The paper says the net interest budget will be reviewed during budget setting to reflect the latest capital programme plans. Markets are anticipating a higher Bank Rate.
findings.matters: Half-year net interest at 81% of the full-year budget, and well above the prior year, is a figure finance directors will test against their own interest assumptions.
findings.quote: with an actual of £380,928 at the end of September (£277,140 in 2025/26).

findings.headline: The HRA is due to repay £9.268 million to the General Fund in 2026/27, with £7.34 million assumed to come from the debt repayment reserve and the remainder refinanced.
findings.detail: The paper sets out the HRA's planned repayment to the General Fund for the year and the assumed funding. HRA debt is forecast to end the year at £57,700k against a £59,900k estimate.
findings.matters: Using a debt repayment reserve to fund an intra-council repayment, with the balance refinanced, shows how an HRA repayment is being funded.
findings.figures: £9.268 million HRA repayment to General Fund; £7.34 million from debt repayment reserve; £57,700k end-of-year HRA debt forecast; £59,900k estimate
findings.quote: The HRA is due to repay £9.268 million to the General Fund in 2026/27.

findings.headline: A PWLB HRA rate 0.4% below the certainty rate is available until March 2027, and £7 million has been borrowed at it since March 2024.
findings.detail: The discounted rate supports local authority borrowing for the Housing Revenue Account. The paper describes it as a window of opportunity for HRA-related borrowing, and says £7 million has been borrowed at the discounted rate to fund the HRA capital programme.
findings.matters: A time-limited PWLB discount for HRA borrowing ends in March 2027, which affects the timing decisions of every council with an HRA capital programme.
findings.figures: 0.4% below certainty rate; £7 million borrowed at discounted rate; available up to March 2027
findings.quote: A PWLB HRA rate which is 0.4% below the certainty rate is available up to March 2027.

findings.headline: The Council held £53.4 million of loans at 30 September 2026, £108,000 less than at 31 March 2026, and expects to borrow up to an additional £8 million in 2026/27.
findings.detail: Long-term borrowing from the PWLB stood at £52,667k at an average rate of 3.64%. The paper says the additional borrowing will part-fund the capital programme. Total debt remained well within the Authorised Limit of £175 million.
findings.matters: A council planning up to £8 million of new borrowing in-year is a funding decision lenders and finance directors track against the capital programme.
findings.figures: £53.4 million total loans; £108,000 reduction; up to £8 million additional borrowing; 3.64% average long-term rate; £175 million Authorised Limit
findings.quote: The Council expects to borrow up to an additional £8 million

findings.headline: Town Centre Regeneration Arcading and Improvement Works recorded £9,720 spent against a £154,700 budget to 30 September 2026, with implementation expected from spring/early summer 2027.
findings.detail: A project manager has been appointed and procurement is progressing. The paper says most professional fees are expected to begin to be drawn down over the coming weeks, and that implementation spend is expected to begin in spring/early summer 2027.
findings.matters: The gap between the approved scheme budget and the expected timing of implementation spend is one that finance officers will be tracking across regeneration schemes.
findings.figures: £9,447,000 scheme budget; £1,000,000 budget 2026/27; £154,700 budget to 30 Sep 26; £9,720 actual to 30 Sep 26
findings.quote: to begin in spring/early summer 2027.

findings.headline: Vehicle Replacement Programme orders have been accelerated to account for 12-18 month refuse vehicle lead times, with three more RCVs to be bought before year end.
findings.detail: The paper says the programme is being reviewed and orders accelerated. Four more RCVs are already ordered from the 2027/28 replacement programme. A revised five-year programme will go to the November Executive.
findings.matters: Lead times for refuse vehicles are pulling spending forward into the current year, which other councils running fleet replacement will face.
findings.figures: £1,255,900 scheme budget; £628,000 budget to 30 Sep 26; £482,952 actual to 30 Sep 26; 12-18 month lead times
findings.quote: The VRP is being reviewed and orders accelerated

findings.headline: Repairs to the Alpha, Bravo and Delta taxiways are completed, with the final project cost expected to be slightly less than the tendered sum.
findings.detail: Payments for the completed taxiway works are due shortly. Runway shoulder works were postponed until spring because of weather, and helipad repairs were completed in spring as part of the wider scope. The paper attributes the lower expected cost to less significant repairs than originally anticipated.
findings.matters: A project finishing under its tendered sum is worth noting, and the postponed runway works show a deadline moving into the next financial year.
findings.figures: £670,000 scheme budget; £329,300 budget to 30 Sep 26; £0 actual to 30 Sep 26
findings.quote: The final project cost is expected to be slightly less than the tendered sum,

findings.headline: The Faraday Link Road professional fees budget is proposed to rise from £410,000 to £500,000 to assess two route options, funded from retained business rates.
findings.detail: Technical investigations identified the need to assess two potential link road routes. The paper says grant of approximately £1.1 million has been secured through Hampshire County Council from the LEP Legacy Reserve Fund, subject to legal agreements. The extra funding covers planning-stage fees only; a further report on construction funding will follow.
findings.matters: A scheme's pre-construction budget rising before planning permission is a pattern other councils planning road or infrastructure schemes will recognise, and the grant split is set out.
findings.figures: £410,000 existing budget; £90,000 additional; £500,000 total; approximately £1.1 million grant
findings.quote: Subsequent technical investigations have identified the need to assess two potential route options for the proposed link road.

findings.headline: The 2026/27 General Fund capital budget is £16,838,000, up from the £12.09 million approved in February after carry-forward and additions.
findings.detail: The Executive approved £12.09 million in February. A £2.04 million carry-forward from 2025/26 was added, along with new schemes and scheme budget increases through the year, including the Town Centre Regeneration Arcading scheme at £9.447 million.
findings.matters: The programme grew substantially during the year through in-year Executive decisions, which is relevant to how other councils track approved versus current capital budgets.
findings.figures: £12.09 million approved 2 February 2026; £2.04 million carry-forward; £2,702,300 2026/27 additions; £16,838,000 total 2026/27 budget
findings.quote: On 2 February 2026, the Executive approved the 2026/27 capital programme of £12.09 million for the General Fund.

findings.headline: General Fund capital spend to 30 September 2026 was £3,435,491, 64% of the £5,393,000 profiled budget for the first half.
findings.detail: The paper reports 64% of the capital programme spent against the profiled budget for the first half of the year, and 20% spent against the full-year budget. It says budgets will be reviewed and re-phased in the forthcoming budget setting process.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the first-half spend rate against the re-phasing the paper says will follow in budget setting.
findings.figures: £3,435,491 actual to 30 Sep 26; £5,393,000 budget to 30 Sep 26; £16,838,000 budget 2026/27; 64% of profiled budget; 20% of total budget
findings.quote: 64% of the capital programme has been spent compared to the profiled budget for the first half of the year.

findings.headline: The revised 2026/27 budget will be available by the end of the calendar year, with the Finance Strategy due in December 2026 and an updated position reported in January 2027.
findings.detail: The paper says monitoring has been increased because of current pressures, and known spending pressures will feed into the Finance Strategy.
findings.matters: The timetable shows when the council will commit to a revised outturn, which the paper says is needed because the half-year position may not hold.
findings.figures: No sums given
findings.quote: The Council is currently working up a revised budget for 2026/27 which will be available by the end of the calendar year.

findings.headline: Interest rates are reported at 3.75% against CPI of 3.10% in August, and the paper says this will weigh on investment performance.
findings.detail: The paper says the council's financial investments will be affected by the fall in interest rates since August 2023 and that inflation remains above target, affecting contract costs.
findings.matters: Lower investment returns alongside above-target inflation are a combination that finance directors will need to reflect in their treasury and budget planning.
findings.figures: Interest rate 3.75%; CPI 3.10% (August)
findings.quote: Interest rates have been reducing since August 2023 and currently sit at 3.75% which will have a downside in terms of the performance of the Councils’ financial investments.

findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility funding of £1.3million is built into the 2026/27 base budget, with the amount expected to rise in the revised budget.
findings.detail: The paper says the final figure remains uncertain, and the revised budget will set the amount.
findings.matters: EPR income is a new central government funding stream, and other councils will be setting their own assumptions about how much to build into base budgets.
findings.figures: £1.3million in base budget
findings.quote: The Council will receive some funding for Extended Producer Responsibility during 2026/27 with a sum of £1.3million built into the base budget.

findings.headline: Trade Waste income is down by almost £91,000 against budget for the year, while the service's net position is £77,000 over budget.
findings.detail: The paper says the income reduction is partly offset by lower tipping fees, and that vehicle repair and hire costs have risen.
findings.matters: A fall in commercial waste income is a signal about business customer demand that councils with similar trade waste services will want to check against their own figures.
findings.figures: Income reduction of almost £91,000; net variation £77,070 (table, £)
findings.quote: The service is seeing a reduction in income against the budget for the year of almost £91,000

findings.headline: Investment property rents are on track to be above budget for the year, partly from newly negotiated leases, while Commercial Estates income is under budget.
findings.detail: The paper says the Commercial Estates income shortfall is offset by lower consultants', legal and management costs. It also says the position on income from property-based services will continue to be monitored.
findings.matters: Two property income streams moving in opposite directions shows how commercial portfolio exposure can differ even within one council.
findings.figures: Investment Properties variation -£61,610 (table, £); Commercial Estates variation -£3,633 (table, £)
findings.quote: Rents are on track to be above budget for the year, partly due to some newly negotiated leases

findings.headline: Bed and breakfast spend in Homelessness is £100,000 under budget, a reduction the paper says has continued into 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper says the reduction has been offset by higher rents payable to private landlords and lower rental income, leaving the service £89,186 under budget overall.
findings.matters: Falling temporary accommodation spend is a demand signal that councils across England are watching as a possible sign of prevention work or changing need.
findings.figures: Bed and breakfast £100,000 under budget; service variation -£89,186 (table, £)
findings.quote: The reduction in Bed and Breakfast spend has continued into this financial year and is currently £100,000 under the budget.

findings.headline: Car park income is £102,000 above budget to 30 September 2026, driven by town centre and coastal parking.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the increase to higher town centre and coastal parking levels. An underspend on business rates has also helped, partly offset by higher maintenance costs.
findings.matters: Parking income is a discretionary income stream, and the paper's attribution to parking levels rather than tariffs is a point other councils with seaside or town centre car parks will compare.
findings.figures: Income £102,000 above budget; service variation -£96,257 (table, £)
findings.quote: Income from users of the Council’s car parks is currently £102,000 more than the budget due to an increase in both town centre and coastal parking levels.

findings.headline: Planning Applications income is almost £130,000 above budget to 30 September 2026, mainly from major applications.
findings.detail: The paper says the income increase comes from major applications bringing in larger fee income, partly offset by higher employee costs.
findings.matters: Planning fee income is volatile and depends on a small number of large schemes, which makes it a useful signal for finance directors judging how much of a surplus will repeat.
findings.figures: Income above budget to date by almost £130,000; variation -£110,929 (table, £); budget to 30 Sep 26 £25,100; actual -£85,829
findings.quote: The income for the year is higher than the budget to date by almost £130,000 which is mainly due to an increase in major applications that bring in larger fee income.

findings.headline: Employer pension contributions paid by Fareham fell from 1 April 2026, following the latest valuation.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the reduction to the pension fund's positive performance, which was passed on to employers at the latest valuation.
findings.matters: A lower employer contribution rate after a valuation is a recurring saving that finance teams at other LGPS employers will want to compare against their own valuation outcomes.
findings.figures: No rate or sum given in the paper
findings.quote: There was a reduction in the employer’s pension contributions that are paid by Fareham which came into effect on 1 April 2026.

findings.headline: The 2026 pay award was agreed at 3.3%, slightly above the 3.2% budget provision, and was backdated to 1 April.
findings.detail: The award was paid in September, backdated to 1 April 2026. The paper describes the difference from budget as slight.
findings.matters: Any pay award above the budgeted rate adds to the base cost of the workforce, and other councils setting 2027/28 budgets will compare their assumptions with this figure.
findings.figures: Pay award 3.3%; budget provision 3.2%
findings.quote: The 2026 pay award was agreed in August at 3.3% and was paid in September (backdated to 1 April).

findings.headline: Employee costs are £183,357 under the £13,078,000 budget to 30 September 2026, mainly from vacancies.
findings.detail: The paper says the underspend comes from vacancies and lower agency and casual spend, with overtime still over budget and usually offset by vacancy savings. The paper's table shows a variance of £183,573 for the same line, a difference of £216 from the text.
findings.matters: Employees are about 60% of gross expenditure, so vacancy-driven savings are a large lever that finance directors elsewhere will want to see.
findings.figures: Underspend £183,357 (text) against budget £13,078,000; table variance -£183,573; budget to 30 Sep 26 £13,078,000; actual £12,894,427
findings.quote: The overall position on employees shows an underspend of £183,357 against a budget of £13,078,000.

findings.headline: A major piece of work has been completed to revise the Vehicle Replacement Programme, which the paper says is expected to affect vehicle costs over time.
findings.detail: The paper calls vehicle running costs the main pressure with management plans in place, and says they remain over budget. It also says the record diesel prices are outside management's control.
findings.matters: A revised replacement programme is a capital and fleet decision that other councils with ageing fleets may be making at the same time.
findings.figures: Diesel prices described as "record levels" (no figure given)
findings.quote: but a major piece of work has been completed to revise the Vehicle Replacement Programme which is expected to have an impact over time.

findings.headline: Waste & Recycling is £197,868 over budget to 30 September 2026, despite an increase in its budget provision for the year.
findings.detail: The overspend reflects vehicle repairs and hire costs to replace vehicles not in service, partly offset by higher income. The paper hopes costs will fall as replacement vehicles bought this year come into use.
findings.matters: The paper's expectation that costs will fall depends on fleet replacement arriving on time, which is a dependency other councils running similar services will want to test.
findings.figures: Budget £3,901,600 (annual); budget to 30 Sep 26 £1,225,900; actual £1,423,768; variation £197,868
findings.quote: It is hoped these costs will have reduced in the latter months of the year as the impact of replacement vehicles purchased starts to be seen.

findings.headline: Streetscene is £175,762 over its budget to 30 September 2026, which the paper attributes mainly to vehicle costs including fuel and vehicle hire.
findings.detail: Streetscene is the only portfolio reported as overspending at the half-year. The paper lists fuel, repairs, hire to replace vehicles under repair, materials and employee costs as the drivers.
findings.matters: Vehicle fuel and hire costs are a pressure other councils with similar fleets will recognise, and the paper ties the overspend to external fuel prices as well as internal fleet decisions.
findings.figures: Budget £1,031,900; actual £1,207,662; variation £175,762 (budget to date and actual shown in £)
findings.quote: Streetscene that is showing as overspending mainly due to higher vehicle costs including fuel and vehicle hire.

findings.headline: The paper anticipates a year-end underspend that would add to reserves, with no drawdown from reserves set for 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper says the 2026/27 budget was set without drawing on reserves, and any underspend will be added to general fund reserves. It repeats the expectation that the year will end with a contribution to reserves, but notes that spending tends to rise in the latter months.
findings.matters: A reserves contribution rather than a drawdown is a change in direction that lenders and other finance teams track closely.
findings.figures: No drawdown from reserves budgeted for 2026/27 (no sum given)
findings.quote: It is anticipated that the overall position will remain as an underspend a the end of the financial year which will mean there would be a contribution to reserves.

findings.headline: General Fund service budgets show a £328k variation under budget to 30 September 2026, against a budget to date of -£200k and actual of -£528k.
findings.detail: The paper says the half-year position is an underspend and that current forecasts predict it will continue to year end. It also says some areas are likely to remain overspent unless changes are made in the revised budget process.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare a half-year underspend of this size on a £18.7m service budget with the year-end outturn reported in January 2027.
findings.figures: Service budget £18,743k; budget to 30 Sep 26 -£200k; actual to 30 Sep 26 -£528k; variation -£328k
findings.quote: Revenue spending plans are currently showing a net underspend for the first half of the financial year.

findings.headline: Government sets a 10-year social housing rent settlement from 2026 at CPI + 1 per cent
findings.detail: The paper says the 10-year rent settlement gives certainty about the annual rent increases that can be applied until 2036. It says this supports longer-term HRA business planning and investment decisions. Rent convergence is also due from 2027/28, at £1 per week rising to £2 per week from 2028/29.
findings.matters: A fixed ten-year rent formula is a long-term income assumption that a finance director or lender would need to reflect in HRA business plans.
findings.figures: Rent settlement: Consumer Price Index + 1 per cent; convergence £1 per week in 2027/28, £2 per week from 2028/29
findings.quote: The government has set a 10-year social housing rent settlement from 2026 at Consumer Price Index + 1 per cent.

findings.headline: Assheton Court capital budget to be re-phased after works started later than planned and extreme weather affected the programme
findings.detail: The paper says work is well underway at Assheton Court. The capital budget will be re-phased to carry forward the 2025/26 budget, because works started later than planned and extreme weather affected the construction programme. Actual spend to 30 September is slightly above the half-year budget.
findings.matters: A scheme with a re-phased budget, because of late start and weather delays, is a timing change a finance director would track against the full-year capital outturn.
findings.figures: Assheton Court base budget £5,200k; budget to 30 Sep £3,000k; actual £3,119k; variation -£119k
findings.quote: the phasing of the capital budget for the scheme will be revised to reflect the budget carry forward from 2025/26 as works started later than originally anticipated and extreme weather has impacted the construction programme.

findings.headline: HRA revenue surplus of £4,423k transferred to the HRA reserve at 30 September 2026, £76k above the half-year budget
findings.detail: Income is £171k above the half-year budget, mainly from 2025/26 service charge adjustments and a Council Housebuilding Support grant rolled forward. The paper says the surplus does not yet reflect year-end corporate recharges and reserve adjustments. It also says the full-year forecast outturn is expected to be in line with budget.
findings.matters: A half-year surplus with a full-year forecast in line with budget shows the reserve position is being moved in line with plan, and the year-end adjustments the paper flags will determine the final figure.
findings.figures: Transfer to/(from) HRA reserve: budget to 30 Sep £4,347k; actual £4,423k; variation £76k; income variation £171k against a base budget of £16,542k
findings.quote: The value of the surplus at the half year point is above the budget set for the first 6 months by £76k.

findings.headline: Revenue repairs expenditure of £2,553k to 30 September 2026 against a £2,445k budget, following the new Voids, Responsive Repairs and Refurbishment partnership
findings.detail: The paper says repairs spend is slightly above budget and attributes this to demand-led service costs and more refurbishment work under the new partnership contract. The paper says these costs are being closely monitored, with enhanced scrutiny of invoiced costs.
findings.matters: A new long-term repairs partnership showing early cost pressure is a risk any council or lender tracking HRA repair costs would want to see.
findings.figures: Revenue repairs expenditure budget to 30 Sep £2,445k; actual £2,553k; variation -£108k; full-year base budget £4,913k
findings.quote: The property repairs and maintenance expenditure is slightly higher than budgeted after the first six months of 2026/27.

findings.headline: HRA capital programme spend of £6,159k to 30 September 2026 against a £5,586k budget, a £573k overspend
findings.detail: The paper reports that the capital programme is overspent at the half-year point, driven mainly by improvement works. The paper links this to a £531k underspend in 2025/26 that was carried forward, and to committed Warm Homes, concrete repair and external rendering work.
findings.matters: A half-year capital overspend against budget, with the paper stating that it is expected to continue, is a variance a finance director would need to see in the year-end capital outturn.
findings.figures: Base budget £13,362k; budget to 30 Sep £5,586k; actual to 30 Sep £6,159k; variation -£573k; improvements £2,564k actual against £2,100k budget (-£464k); 2025/26 underspend £531k
findings.quote: The Housing Revenue Account Capital Programme is overspent against the budget overall after the first 6 months of 2026/27, as set out in the following table.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Awaab's Law (effective October 2025) introduced statutory repair timescales for social housing; council recruited new Property Inspector role.
findings.detail: Awaab's Law came into effect in October 2025 and introduced statutory timescales for social housing repairs, particularly for damp and mould, with requirements for tenant communication throughout repair stages. Fareham responded by recruiting a new Property Inspector to review housing stock and ensure timely resolution of damp and mould issues.
findings.matters: New regulatory duties create operational costs and compliance risk; failure to meet statutory timescales could trigger enforcement action and damage the council's credibility as a housing provider.
findings.figures: One new Property Inspector position created; statute effective October 2025
findings.quote: A new Property Inspector has been recruited, and they will have responsibility for accurately reviewing the Council's Housing stock and documenting cases of damp and mould to ensure they are resolved in a timely manner.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Medium-term funding gaps in 2027/28 and 2028/29 will require drawing down Council reserves to address shortfalls.
findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Strategy for 2025-2030 predicts funding gaps in both 2027/28 and 2028/29, with government funding expected to help balance the budget only by 2029/30. The council will need to use reserves to support the Local Government Reorganisation programme through April 2028, and further projects are anticipated to require additional reserve depletion to address shortfalls in the next two years.
findings.matters: Planned reserve drawdown indicates liquidity constraint and reduces financial flexibility to respond to emergencies, service pressures, or unexpected costs.
findings.figures: Funding gaps in 2027/28 and 2028/29; reserves required through April 2028 for LGR; £271,000 savings in 2025/26 from Opportunities Plan
findings.quote: Going forward, there will be a requirement to use Council reserves to support the LGR programme through to April 2028. The current Opportunities Plan will still need to be used to address the shortfall in the next two financial years.

findings.headline: Four additional control area weaknesses identified requiring enhancement including purchasing card authorisation
findings.detail: The audit opinion identifies specific governance gaps requiring remediation: vehicle record maintenance in Streetscene, controls over repair invoice verification, purchasing card authorisation processes, and VAT treatment consistency. These gaps span procurement, asset management and financial processes.
findings.matters: Multiple identified control deficiencies across different functions indicate broader governance maturity issues affecting financial stewardship and compliance.
findings.figures: 4 priority areas identified
findings.quote: Additional areas noted this year where further action will enhance the adequacy and effectiveness of governance, risk management and control include: a. Maintenance of records relating to vehicles within the Streetscene Directorate b. Controls and processes for the calculation and verification of repairs invoices c. The authorisation process for purchasing cards d. Greater clarity and consistency on the treatment of VAT

findings.headline: Audit recommendation implementation rate fell to 56% from 74%, with 35% still in progress
findings.detail: Of 108 essential or important recommendations reviewed, only 56% have been implemented or closed, with 35% in progress. This is a material decline from 2024/25 when 74% were implemented. The council has introduced action-by dates for new recommendations in attempt to improve completion rates.
findings.matters: Low recommendation implementation rates extend exposure to identified control weaknesses. Declining performance suggests services are slower to remediate issues and weaker accountability for control improvement.
findings.figures: 56% implemented vs 74% prior year; 35% in progress; 108 recommendations reviewed
findings.quote: Of the 108 recommendations reviewed 56% of recommendations followed up were signed off by the audit team and a further 35% were being progressed. This represents a drop in performance from the previous year.

findings.headline: Payroll system error caused £2,117 overpayment to elected members that only audit detected
findings.detail: The system applied both a Councillor Allowance and Employee Allowance simultaneously to three elected members in August 2025, resulting in a £2,117 overpayment. The error was only identified through audit testing, suggesting insufficient reconciliation controls in payroll.
findings.matters: Payroll overpayments represent direct cash loss and indicate control gaps in routine financial systems. That audit was needed to identify the error suggests weak preventive controls.
findings.figures: £2,117 overpayment in single pay run
findings.quote: The Payroll, Pensions and Employee Expenses audit noted 1 error. This related to the overpayment to three elected members in the August 2025 pay run as the system had applied both a Councillor and Employee Allowance in error. The total value of the overpayment was £2,117.

findings.headline: VAT non-compliance errors across multiple departments triggering council-wide audit
findings.detail: VAT errors found in four separate audits: £1,600 not reclaimed in grant certification, £1,032 net VAT impact from 18 errors in Housing Rents invoicing, £580 output tax and £21 input tax omitted from Vehicle Management, plus £119.80 in further miscoding. The council has commissioned a full council-wide VAT audit for 2026/27 to address the systemic treatment issues.
findings.matters: Systemic VAT errors across multiple departments reduce cash recovery and indicate weak financial control over tax compliance. Unrealised tax recovery directly impacts council finances.
findings.figures: £1,600 grant cert; £1,032 housing rents (18 errors); £580+£21+£119.80 vehicle management
findings.quote: A number of issues were noted across various reviews and services in relation to the treatment of VAT. In response to this a full Council wide VAT audit has been included within the 2026/27 Audit Plan.

findings.headline: Vehicle Management given Minimal Assurance with no reliable fleet dataset and critical compliance failures
findings.detail: The Vehicle Management audit received Minimal Assurance (the lowest rating) with 3 Essential, 12 Important and 2 Necessary recommendations. The council has no complete or reliable fleet dataset with conflicting records, missing information, and weak reconciliation. Critical compliance risks (tax and MOT) have already occurred. Four Essential recommendations from follow-up are still in progress. The area last received a Strong opinion 7 years ago.
findings.matters: Minimal assurance on core operational assets indicates material control failures. Fleet is a significant council asset; unresolved essential recommendations suggest slow remediation and ongoing operational risk.
findings.figures: 3 Essential, 12 Important, 2 Necessary recommendations; 4 Essential outstanding; last Strong opinion 2019
findings.quote: The Vehicle Management Audit was given 'Minimal Assurance' after 3 Essential, 12 Important and 2 Necessary recommendations were made. The key findings were that there is no complete or reliable fleet dataset, with conflicting records, missing information and weak reconciliation processes, alongside poor inventory, procurement and financial record management. Additionally critical compliance (tax and MOT) and operational risks exist and had occurred

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Outturn Report v2
findings.headline: General Fund reserves will be needed for Local Government Reorganisation costs and other major projects amid identified forward funding gaps
findings.detail: The council has identified a funding gap for 2027/28-2028/29 in its Medium-Term Finance Strategy. While the 2025/26 underspend of £566,321 provides some relief, the council explicitly states reserves must be held to fund Local Government Reorganisation initial costs and "accelerated corporate priorities". The £125m Town Centre Masterplan is also competing for General Fund reserve funding.
findings.matters: Multiple competing demands on reserves (forward budget gaps, LGR costs, major capital projects) reduce the council's financial flexibility and borrowing capacity. This constrains the council's ability to respond to unexpected financial pressures.
findings.figures: 2025/26 underspend £566,321; funding gap identified for 2027/28-2028/29; £125m Town Centre Masterplan
findings.quote: However, there remains a need to be cautious as the Council's overall reserves position will need to be kept under review as they may need to help fund the accelerated corporate priorities and/or the initial costs of Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Outturn Report v2
findings.headline: Income volatility across multiple services creates ongoing budget planning uncertainty
findings.detail: The council's outturn reveals significant income variations across services: Planning income exceeded budget by £236,000, Investment Properties by £124,000 (primarily from rent reviews), while Trade Waste fell £50,000 short. The council explicitly states this volatility requires close monitoring of future budget positions, indicating heightened uncertainty about forward income reliability.
findings.matters: Volatile income streams make sustainable budget planning and service delivery levels harder to forecast reliably. For a lender, this creates uncertainty about the council's ability to maintain financial stability and meet obligations in changing economic conditions.
findings.figures: Planning applications income £236,000 over budget; Investment Properties income £124,000 over budget; Trade Waste income £50,000 under budget
findings.quote: the volatility of income and expenditure being seen this year means that we will need to continue to closely monitor the budget position for 2026/27 and the effect of this will be reviewed in the Medium-Term Finance Strategy later in 2027

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Outturn Report v2
findings.headline: Waste and Recycling Service showing largest service overspend of £290,878 driven by aging vehicle fleet maintenance costs
findings.detail: The Waste and Recycling Service delivered the largest service overspend in the council year, totalling £290,878. The primary driver is a £62,000 overspend on vehicle repairs and maintenance attributed to an aging fleet, compounded by additional fuel and hire costs. The service also experienced lower-than-expected income. This appears to be a structural problem rather than one-off variation.
findings.matters: This is the single largest service overspend in the council and signals potential capital underinvestment in essential service delivery vehicles. The aging fleet represents an ongoing cost pressure that will recur and may eventually require significant capital expenditure for replacement.
findings.figures: Waste and Recycling total overspend £290,878; vehicle repairs and maintenance overspend £62,000; employee expenses overspend £50,000
findings.quote: The main reason for the overspends was around the vehicles used for the services that was showing an increase of £62,000 over the increased budget mainly due to repair and maintenance of vehicles due to an aging fleet

findings.headline: HRA capital programme spent only 77% of budget (£12.3M actual vs £15.9M budget) with £3.6M carried forward to future years and delivery being reviewed
findings.detail: Capital spending underspent across Improvements and Modernisations (£2.986M actual vs £3.517M budget) and New Builds and Regeneration (£7.489M actual vs £10.387M budget). The report states 'This area of spend will be reviewed again over the coming year as the next detailed programme of works is compiled', indicating the council may not yet have confirmed how it will deploy the carried-forward budgets. Major projects like Assheton Court (£7.2M) and Birks regeneration are planned but timing remains uncertain.
findings.matters: Large capital commitments create future debt and finance charge obligations; inability to deploy budgets as planned suggests contractor, grant, or planning delays that could extend project timelines and increase costs
findings.figures: Budget £15.9M, actual spend £12.3M, carryover £3.605M; Assheton Court £7.296M in 2025/26
findings.quote: The underspent budgets against Improvements and Modernisation and New Builds are proposed to be carried forward as future high levels of spend are still anticipated. This area of spend will be reviewed again over the coming year as the next detailed programme of works is compiled.

findings.headline: Internal borrowing totalling £11.268M falls due in 2026/27, requiring a refinancing or repayment decision that has not yet been made
findings.detail: £9.268M borrowed internally in 2012 and £2M borrowed internally in 2025 both fall due in 2026/27 (the 2025 tranche in 2026). The council has not yet decided whether to refinance or repay, noting 'Detailed analysis and evaluation on the possible re-financing and repayment options of the £11,268,000 will be carried out in anticipation of this as part of the budgeting process for 2027/28'. The timing and approach will materially affect HRA borrowing costs.
findings.matters: A decision to repay could create cash pressure; a decision to refinance will depend on prevailing interest rates. Either way, this is a significant rebalancing of the debt portfolio that will determine debt service costs for the next decade
findings.figures: £11.268M falling due (£9.268M from 2012 at maturity 2027, £2M from 2025 at maturity 2026)
findings.quote: The Internal Borrowing taken out in 2012 and in 2025 falls due for repayment later in the 2026/27 financial year. Detailed analysis and evaluation on the possible re-financing and repayment options of the £11,268,000 will be carried out in anticipation of this as part of the budgeting process for 2027/28.

findings.headline: HRA borrowing is set to increase by £4.4M in 2026/27 for new build projects, with future finance charges rising as a result
findings.detail: The council plans new PWLB borrowing of £4.4M in 2026/27 to fund new build capital projects. The report explicitly states this 'will result in additional revenue finance charges to the HRA in future years', but does not quantify those additional charges. Current total HRA debt stands at £58.268M across multiple tranches with varying maturity dates.
findings.matters: Increasing debt service costs will reduce HRA surplus and constrain financial flexibility, particularly when combined with rising regulatory cost pressures
findings.figures: £4.4M new borrowing planned 2026/27; total current HRA borrowing £58.268M; total interest payable 2025/26 was £2.193M
findings.quote: It should also be noted that borrowing is set to increase by £4.4M million in 2026/27, which is attributed to new build capital projects. This, along with future capital new build expenditure, will result in additional revenue finance charges to the HRA in future years.

findings.headline: Awaabs Law is driving new and ongoing responsive repairs costs, with staffing already increased by £181k and further regulatory phases coming in 2026 and 2027
findings.detail: From 27 October 2025, new timeframes apply to investigate and fix certain hazards. Fareham has already increased responsive repairs establishment by £181,482 to recruit a Responsive Repairs Manager, Property Surveyor, and 1.4 Repairs Admin Officers. The report states 'Future resourcing implications for the housing repairs and maintenance and administrative services...will continue to be reviewed', indicating cost pressures remain uncertain and may grow.
findings.matters: Regulatory-driven cost inflation that is not yet fully costed and continues to be under review reduces HRA financial predictability and could threaten reserves or require rent increases if revenue does not keep pace
findings.figures: £181,482 staffing increase; responsive repairs expenditure £4.75M for the year
findings.quote: Under Awaabs Law new requirements have become operational from 27 October 2025, introducing timeframes to investigate and fix certain hazards. Further phases in 2026 and 2027 cover further hazards and health and safety measures. The responsive repairs establishment has already been increased by £181,482 recruiting a new Responsive Repairs Manager, Property Surveyor, and 1.4 Repairs Admin Officers providing additional staffing resources to meet these needs.

findings.headline: £4.4 million HRA borrowing planned for 2026/27 for new build housing capital projects
findings.detail: No Housing Revenue Account borrowing was required in 2025/26, but the council plans to increase HRA borrowing by £4.4m in 2026/27 specifically for new build capital projects. This represents a significant shift in the HRA debt position.
findings.matters: A lender tracking council debt trends needs to know about committed future borrowing increases and the assets they are financing
findings.figures: 2025/26 HRA borrowing: £0. 2026/27 planned: £4.4m
findings.quote: No HRA borrowing was required in 2025/26 but is set to increase by £4.4 million in 2026/27 for new build capital projects.

findings.headline: Disabled Facilities Grants delivery stalled by Hampshire County Council occupational therapy team resourcing issues
findings.detail: The council underspent £510k of a £1.066m budget for this statutory service because referrals from HCC's occupational therapy team were slower than expected. The underspend reflects waiting times in an external service the council cannot directly control. The paper describes this as due to HCC resourcing challenges in assessment.
findings.matters: The council's ability to deliver a statutory service depends on another authority's staffing levels; this creates uncontrollable delivery risk
findings.figures: Disabled Facilities Grants: £1.066m budget, £0.556m spent, £0.510m underspend
findings.quote: Referrals from HCC have been slower than expected due to resourcing challenges, resulting in the reported underspend.

findings.headline: Strategic investment fund holds £1.2 million embedded loss that will hit the General Fund if government extends statutory accounting override after 2029
findings.detail: The council holds £12m in externally-managed pooled funds, currently valued at £10.747m, with a £1.2m loss held in an unusable reserve. A statutory override prevents this loss from impacting the General Fund accounts, but the override expires 4 April 2029. The paper notes there is a risk the government may not extend it.
findings.matters: If the accounting treatment changes in 2029 without replacement funding, the council must absorb £1.2m through the General Fund revenue account
findings.figures: £12m invested, £10.747m current value, £1.2m notional loss; statutory override expires 1 April 2029
findings.quote: The notional loss from the initial £12 million investment is held in an unusable reserve on the Council's balance sheet. However, there is a risk that the government may change this.

findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio value declined £2.2 million, with half of ten properties losing value
findings.detail: The council's commercial investment properties (industrial, retail, childcare) fell from £11.155m to £9.015m in value during the year. This was part of a total portfolio decline of £1.862m across all property holdings. Five of the ten commercial investment properties decreased in value. The paper attributes this to market sentiment linked to rental income and lease terms.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's exposure to property market deterioration and the income risk if rents fall or leases terminate
findings.figures: Commercial investments: £11.155m (2025) to £9.015m (2026), a £2.2m decline. Total portfolio: £66.328m to £64.466m
findings.quote: Since 2025 the Fair Value of this portfolio has decreased by £1,605,000. Five of the properties increased in value whereas five reduced in value.

findings.headline: Council maintains £500k reserve for pooled investment fund losses; accounting override extended to April 2029
findings.detail: The council has experienced unrealised losses on pooled investment funds (part of the strategic portfolio) and maintains a £500k reserve to mitigate accounting impacts. The statutory override allowing this treatment has been extended to 1 April 2029, indicating the council expects material ongoing volatility in fund valuations through 2029.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the council's investment portfolio has suffered losses, tying up a £500k reserve. The extended override period signals continued vulnerability to further volatility, which is material given the council's stated dependency on investment returns.
findings.figures: Reserve £500,000. Override extended to 1 April 2029.
findings.quote: The Council has maintained a reserve of £500,000 to mitigate the impact of the statutory override on accounting for gains and losses on pooled investment funds which has been extended until 1st April 2029

findings.headline: Council debt forecast to rise from £66.2m to £80m by 2030, with expectation of being permanent long-term borrower
findings.detail: Gross debt is projected to rise from £66.2m in 2026 to £70.5m in 2027, £79.7m in 2029, and £80m in 2030 to fund the capital programme. The council states it expects to be a long-term borrower with persistent capital needs. While forecasts indicate borrowing will remain below the liability benchmark, rising debt combined with declining investment returns (separate theme) raises structural sustainability concerns.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand whether rising debt is sustainable given the council's structural income pressures. Permanent borrowing combined with falling investment returns creates a concerning dynamic.
findings.quote: Debt at 31 March 2026 is projected to be higher due to borrowing externally to fund the capital programme.

findings.headline: Investment returns falling from 4.7% to 3.4% while council explicitly depends on investment income to balance its revenue budget
findings.detail: The council states it is dependent on profit-generating investment activity to achieve a balanced revenue budget. However, net investment returns are declining sharply: 4.7% in 2024/25, falling to 3.4% forecast for 2026/27. Commercial property returns are falling even more steeply from 5.5% to 3.6%. Absolute investment income is declining from £5,390k to £4,608k. With Bank Rate forecast to fall to 3.25%, returns will continue to erode.
findings.matters: Declining investment income while structurally dependent on it creates a material sustainability risk. If property values or rents fall further, the council's ability to balance its revenue budget is jeopardized.
findings.figures: Total investment returns: 4.7% (2024/25), 4.2% (2025/26), 3.4% (2026/27). Commercial property: 5.5%, 4.7%, 3.6%. Investment income falling from £5,390k to £4,608k.
findings.quote: The Council is dependent on profit generating investment activity to achieve a balanced revenue budget.

findings.headline: Significant asset management repair backlog not yet reflected in capital programme
findings.detail: The strategy acknowledges that the full costs of Civic Offices asset management, car park asset management, and public conveniences have not been incorporated. Additionally, 'spending pressures including repair and refurbishment, or replacement works to all Council assets have also yet to be added to the capital programme'.
findings.matters: Deferred asset maintenance creates future spending shocks and indicates how much revenue capacity is genuinely available for other priorities.
findings.figures: Four named projects with costs not yet included; unquantified assets requiring repair and replacement
findings.quote: Spending pressures including repair and refurbishment, or replacement works to all Council assets have also yet to be added to the capital programme.

findings.headline: Financing costs are rising and will consume 11% of General Fund net revenue by 2029/30
findings.detail: The cost of servicing capital debt (interest and Minimum Revenue Provision) is growing from 9% of General Fund revenue in 2026/27 to 11% by 2029/30. This represents an increasing claim on operational resources and leaves less headroom for service delivery pressures.
findings.matters: Lenders assess debt sustainability by the proportion of revenue consumed by financing costs. An upward trend indicates tightening financial flexibility.
findings.figures: 2026/27: £1,400k (9% of net revenue stream); 2029/30: £1,625k (11% of net revenue stream)
findings.quote: Due to the very long-term nature of capital expenditure and financing, the revenue budget implications of expenditure incurred in the next few years will extend for up to 30 years into the future.

findings.headline: Five major corporate priorities have limited or no funding in the capital programme
findings.detail: Town Centre Regeneration, Civic Offices Asset Management, Daedalus infrastructure investment, Environment Strategy, and Fareham Park Vision are all identified as corporate priorities by the Executive, but the Council explicitly states there is minimal or no capital provision for them yet. Separate reports will address their financial implications 'in coming months', meaning costs are not yet quantified.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the full scope of Council commitments. Unquantified priority spending could emerge as unfunded deficits or require unexpected borrowing.
findings.figures: Five named schemes with 'currently limited provision' or undefined funding needs
findings.quote: There is currently limited provision in the programme for the full funding that may be needed for the Town Centre Regeneration, the Civic Offices Asset Management Plan, infrastructure investment at Daedalus, the Environment Strategy or Fareham Park Vision.

findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio has lost £6 million in value since purchase, with further rental declines expected
findings.detail: The Council's commercial property investment portfolio, purchased for £39.8 million between 2013 and 2019, is now valued at £33.8 million (March 2025). The document explicitly warns that further downward rental adjustments are anticipated, particularly in the retail sector where lease cycles and market changes are driving value erosion.
findings.matters: Lenders need visibility of Council asset quality and income reliability. Continued property value decline and falling rental income reduce both security and cash generation.
findings.figures: Portfolio purchase price £39.8 million, March 2025 valuation £33.8 million (£6 million decline); further rental adjustments anticipated
findings.quote: The cumulative purchase price of the portfolio stands at £39.8 million compared to its most recent valuation in March 2025 of £33.8 million, a reduction of £6 million...Although gross rents have increased since March 2022 further downward rental adjustments are anticipated in the coming years.

findings.headline: Over two-thirds of capital programme funding relies on resources not yet confirmed
findings.detail: The Council estimates £89.3 million total resources available but acknowledges that £61 million—nearly two-thirds of the funding pool—depends on future capital receipts, grants, and revenue contributions that have not yet been secured. If these do not materialise, the strategy explicitly states the programme will need to be scaled back or the Council will need to borrow more.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether committed capital spending rests on actual resources or speculative future income, and what happens if forecasts slip.
findings.figures: Total resources £89.3 million, unallocated £2.3 million; unsecured resources £61 million
findings.quote: The forecast surplus of resources is limited and relies partly on resources that have not yet been secured (such as future capital receipts and grants as well as continued revenue contributions towards capital investment), totalling £61 million.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Audit - Audit Results Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Working paper quality issues in major balance areas resulted in scale fee variations and audit delays.
findings.detail: EY identified that working papers for Leases, Receipts in Advance, and PPE were of insufficient quality, representing significant and material balances. This required additional auditor and officer time and resulted in a proposed scale fee variation. Quality of working papers is described as requiring improvement.
findings.matters: Poor working paper support and documentation for material balance areas indicates weak finance function capability and internal controls, increasing audit risk and costs.
findings.figures: Scale fee variation proposed for additional work on IFRS 16 Leases, PPE, and IAS 19
findings.quote: working papers and supporting evidence were generally of a good standard, but as noted in the Control Observations section on page 9, we identified a number of issues with the Council's working papers for Leases, Receipts in Advance and for PPE. These represent significant and material balances within the financial statements. Improvement in these working papers is required

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Audit - Audit Results Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Annual Governance Statement submitted 4 months late; narrative statement did not accompany draft accounts as required.
findings.detail: The financial statements were published by the 30 June deadline, but the Narrative Statement was not provided until 16 October 2025. EY notes this should be presented alongside the draft financial statements by 30 June under the Accounts and Audit Regulations.
findings.matters: Late submission of governance statements suggests weak compliance with statutory deadlines and potential capacity or process issues in the finance function.
findings.figures: Deadline: 30 June 2025; Narrative Statement received: 16 October 2025 (107 days late)
findings.quote: The financial statements were published by the 30th June 2025 deadline set out in the Accounts and Audit Regulations. However, the Council did not provide a copy of the Narrative Statement until 16 October. This should be presented alongside the draft financial statements by 30 June.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Audit - Audit Results Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Pension liability calculation contained material error requiring re-audit after corrected actuary report.
findings.detail: The actuary's initial IAS 19 assessment contained an error in the May 2024 investment return figure resulting in approximately 1% understatement of closing asset figures. EY had to re-perform significant procedures following receipt of the corrected report.
findings.matters: Pension liability is a material balance on the council's balance sheet. An actuary error of this magnitude that required audit re-work signals potential gaps in management's financial reporting oversight and validation procedures.
findings.figures: Approximately 1% understatement in closing pension asset figures due to actuary error
findings.quote: The IAS 19 assessment initially provided by the Council's actuary was incorrect. This was due to an error on the part of the actuary, and specifically a discrepancy in the May 2024 investment return figure which resulted in an approximate 1% understatement of closing asset figures... resulting in the need to re-perform those procedures following receipt of the updated IAS 19 report from the actuary

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Audit - Audit Results Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Fixed asset controls failed to detect or prevent errors from prior years still embedded in records.
findings.detail: The Fixed Asset Register had discrepancies with the General Ledger that appeared to stem from failure to regularly reconcile these records. Investigation found differences carried forward from at least 2020/21 (Wickham Cemetery missed entirely in prior year). Despite management introducing new reconciliation procedures, additional errors were not detected by the Council—EY found assets recorded as 2024/25 disposals that were actually disposed in 2023/24, and an asset recorded as disposed that remained in the Council's possession.
findings.matters: Asset register errors spanning multiple years that management did not detect indicate weak governance over fixed asset accountability, a material concern for collateral valuation or grant compliance.
findings.figures: £121k asset misclassified as disposal; errors present only in FAR spreadsheet with GL figures correct; disposal schedule included assets from 2023/24
findings.quote: Our review of the Fixed Asset Register (FAR) identified immaterial differences between the FAR and the General Ledger (and therefore the financial statements) for multiple assets... This appears to be caused by a failure to regularly revisit the FAR and perform a regular reconciliation between the FAR and General Ledger

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Audit - Audit Results Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Material grant misclassification of £1.192m shows inadequate evidence retention for significant balance areas.
findings.detail: EY identified a £1.192m misclassification of non-ringfenced grants from Receipts in Advance to grants credited to the CIES. They note continued challenges auditing Receipts in Advance, including batch journal postings requiring resampling. The council was unable to provide timely audit evidence.
findings.matters: A £1.192m classification error affecting revenue recognition indicates weak control procedures around grant recording and inadequate documentation systems for material transactions.
findings.figures: £1.192m misclassification; threshold for reporting misstatements £70k
findings.quote: We found that the Council's Expected Credit Losses calculation had incorrectly applied a percentage to aged debtors exceeding 3 years... We identified a misclassification of non-ringfenced grants from Receipts in Advance to grants credited to the CIES totaling £1.192m

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Audit - Audit Results Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Audit opinion remains qualified: council continues recovery from prior-year disclaimers and has not yet rebuilt sufficient assurance.
findings.detail: The council issued disclaimers on 2023/24 and 2022/23 opinions. For 2024/25, EY has gained increased but still insufficient assurance and is considering a qualified opinion rather than a disclaimer. Key gaps remain in PPE, Receipts in Advance, and reserves because prior-year opinions were disclaimed.
findings.matters: A qualified or disclaimed audit opinion signals that the council's financial statements cannot be relied upon as presenting a true and fair view, a material risk for any lender.
findings.figures: Backstop date for final opinion: 27 February 2026
findings.quote: we have not yet collected sufficient evidence to have reasonable assurance over all in-year movements and closing balances. As a result of the disclaimer of opinion on the 2023/24 financial statements, we have not collected assurance over some brought forward balances

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Audit - Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: HRA borrowing increased by £3.85m to finance capital, with auditor noting a material shortfall would exist without this borrowing.
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account incurred a £3.85m borrowing increase primarily to fund new build projects in the capital programme. The auditor explicitly states: 'This suggests there is a significant and material shortfall had the borrowing not been available, and use of borrowing to continue to support capital spend is not likely to be a feasible response to financial pressure in the short or medium term.' The council has begun implementing an HRA-specific Opportunities Plan to mitigate financial risks.
findings.matters: HRA borrowing to finance operating/capital deficits signals structural cash flow pressure. The auditor's comment that continued borrowing is not feasible indicates the HRA faces real financial constraints. This matters to a lender evaluating the council's ability to service existing debt and manage financial pressures.
findings.figures: HRA borrowing increase £3.85m; HRA 2024-25 net expenditure £14.7m against income £16.1m.
findings.quote: HRA borrowing has increased by £3.85m mainly to finance the new build projects in the capital programme, This suggests there is a significant and material shortfall had the borrowing not been available, and use of borrowing to continue to support capital spend is not likely to be a feasible response to financial pressure in the short or medium term.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - External Audit - Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: The auditor has not yet gained full assurance over the 2024-25 financial statements; a disclaimer of opinion was issued on 2023-24 and a qualified opinion is more likely for 2024-25.
findings.detail: The council received a disclaimer of opinion on 2023-24 financial statements. For 2024-25, despite assurance improving, the auditor has not collected sufficient evidence over all in-year movements and closing balances. The auditor is considering whether to issue a qualified (except for) opinion rather than another disclaimer, but states it is more likely to be disclaimed.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion or qualified opinion signals material gaps in audit assurance, meaning the external auditor cannot provide reasonable assurance over significant balances and transactions. This undermines confidence in the reliability of the council's financial position to a prospective lender.
findings.figures: 2023-24: disclaimer of opinion. 2024-25: qualified except for opinion possible, but disclaimer more likely.
findings.quote: Although the level of assurance gained has increased, we have not collected sufficient evidence to have reasonable assurance over all in-year movements and closing balances. As a result of the disclaimer of opinion on the 2023/24 financial statements, we do not have assurance over some brought forward balances from 2023/24 where we did not gain assurance (the opening balances).

findings.paper_title: R05 - FINAL Treasury Management Strategy & Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Reserve of £500,000 maintained to manage fair value volatility in pooled investment funds, statutory override extended to April 2029
findings.detail: Council continues to hold a dedicated reserve to mitigate the accounting impact of unrealised losses on strategic pooled funds. The temporary statutory override allowing councils to defer recognition of these losses in the General Fund has been extended to 1 April 2029.
findings.matters: Shows active management of known investment portfolio volatility and appropriate reserve provisioning for the extent of pooled fund exposure, relevant to peer comparison of investment strategy robustness.
findings.figures: £500,000 reserve; override extension to 1st April 2029
findings.quote: The Council has maintained a reserve of £500,000 to mitigate the impact of the statutory override on accounting for gains and losses on pooled investment funds which has been extended until 1st April 2029

findings.paper_title: R05 - FINAL Treasury Management Strategy & Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Time limit for secured investments reduced from 25 years to 10 years
findings.detail: Tightens the permitted maturity profile for secured investments, moving from a 25-year horizon to a 10-year maximum. This represents a more conservative approach to counterparty credit risk exposure.
findings.matters: Shows treasury risk management tightening, reducing duration exposure and counterparty credit risk on longer-dated secured positions.
findings.figures: 25 years to 10 years (15-year reduction)
findings.quote: the time limit for secured investments has been reduced from 25 years to 10 years

findings.paper_title: R05 - FINAL Treasury Management Strategy & Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Counterparty limit for local authorities and government entities increased from £4 million to £5 million
findings.detail: Minor amendment to approved counterparties policy increases the permitted exposure to individual local authority and government counterparties from £4m to £5m.
findings.matters: Reflects operational adjustment in day-to-day cash management and inter-authority lending capacity under the investment strategy.
findings.figures: £4 million to £5 million limit increase
findings.quote: the counterparty limit for local authorities and government entities has been increased from £4 million to £5 million

findings.paper_title: R05 - FINAL Treasury Management Strategy & Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Counterparty limit for loans to merging local authorities set at unlimited amount where merger is government-announced
findings.detail: New policy provision reflects Local Government Reorganisation context. Where government has announced this Council will merge with a borrowing authority and the loan repays post-merger, the counterparty limit becomes unlimited instead of subject to the usual caps.
findings.matters: Directly signals this council is part of local government reorganisation planning and that treasury policy is being adapted to accommodate merger-related inter-authority lending.
findings.figures: Unlimited counterparty limit for merger scenario (versus standard £5 million limit)
findings.quote: The counterparty limit for loans to local authorities will be increased to an unlimited amount where (a) the government has announced that this Council will merge with the borrowing authority and (b) the loan is scheduled to be repaid after the expected date of the merger.

findings.paper_title: R05 - FINAL Treasury Management Strategy & Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Council will consider long-term loans from sources beyond the Public Works Loan Board, moving from PWLB-only funding
findings.detail: Previously all long-term borrowing has been from PWLB. The strategy now signals openness to alternative funding sources for long-term loans, suggesting a shift toward funding diversification.
findings.matters: Signals potential strategy shift toward funding optionality and counterparty diversification, affecting future cost of capital and refinancing flexibility.
findings.figures: £70.5 million expected borrowing at end 2026/27
findings.quote: The Council has previously raised all of its long-term borrowing from the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) but will consider long-term loans from other sources.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Budgets & Finance Strategy Reports & Appendices
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation implementation costs of £500,000 allocated for 3 years create a new sustained cost pressure.
findings.detail: The council has determined that despite expected savings post-LGR, there will be implementation costs incurred before the reorganisation completes. A £500,000 allocation for 3 years (2025/26 onwards) has been added to support staff preparation and change management related to the structural reform.
findings.matters: A large structural reform of local government creates near-term costs and uncertainty about post-2028 financial position. The lender needs to understand whether the council's post-LGR financial projections are realistic and whether this reorganisation risk is adequately reflected in the council's forward plan.
findings.figures: £500,000 allocated from 2025/26 for 3 years for Local Government Reorganisation implementation costs
findings.quote: Although the case identifies that savings will be made post LGR, there are implementation costs that will be incurred before then. Therefore, £500,000 is now being allocated from 2025/26 for 3 years to cover those costs.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Budgets & Finance Strategy Reports & Appendices
findings.headline: General fund reserves forecast to decline to 5% of gross revenue expenditure, below the council's own minimum policy of 7.5%.
findings.detail: The council has previously agreed that the spending reserve should represent at least 7.5% of gross revenue expenditure. The forecasts in this report show this level is expected not to fall below 5%, meaning reserves are declining relative to policy and approaching a lower-than-desired buffer.
findings.matters: Reserve adequacy is a core credit metric for lenders. A reserve buffer below the council's own stated minimum indicates financial headroom is eroding, especially given the identified future funding gaps that will consume reserves further.
findings.figures: Target reserve: 7.5% of gross revenue expenditure; forecast: not to fall below 5%
findings.quote: A key mitigation is that the Executive has previously agreed that the balance on the spending reserve should equate to at least 7.5% of gross revenue expenditure to help protect the Council from extraordinary events. The forecasts in this report expect this level not to fall below 5%.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Budgets & Finance Strategy Reports & Appendices
findings.headline: Homelessness service costs previously exceeded £2 million and are only now being managed down by £400,000, demonstrating past loss of control over a major cost centre.
findings.detail: The housing team identified a significant budget pressure on bed and breakfast expenses for the homeless that had reached over £2m. A rigorous review has reduced costs by £400,000, but the service remains large and volatile. The document notes the Homelessness Prevention Grant is being restructured in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A service that lost cost control at £2m represents operational weakness and demand risk. Even with recent improvements, demand-led spending on homelessness (a national pressure affecting all councils) remains a financial vulnerability for the lender's borrower.
findings.figures: Bed and breakfast expenses reached over £2 million; costs cut by £400,000 per year through service review
findings.quote: Previously it has been highlighted that there was a significant budget pressure in relation to bed and breakfast expenses for the homeless which had seen costs increase to over £2million. The Housing team have since been carrying out a rigorous holistic review of this service and as a result have managed to significantly cut the cost of providing the service by a further £400,000 a year.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Budgets & Finance Strategy Reports & Appendices
findings.headline: Streetscene repairs and vehicle hire budget increased by £607,000 in 2025/26 and £374,000 in 2026/27 due to ageing fleet
findings.detail: The council has identified ongoing issues from having an ageing vehicle fleet in streetscene services. Repairs and vehicle hire budgets are rising significantly, with the council noting that these costs are expected to continue decreasing in future years, implying a capital replacement programme is planned to address the issue.
findings.matters: Fleet aging signals deferred maintenance and upcoming capital replacement needs. A lender needs to know whether the council has funded its asset replacement strategy. Temporary cost spikes can become structural if the underlying capital investment is not made.
findings.figures: Repairs and vehicle hire budget increase: £607,000 in 2025/26; £374,000 in 2026/27
findings.quote: The budgets have been updated within the Streetscene service by a significant amount to reflect the ongoing issues from having an ageing fleet. Repairs and vehicle hire budget will increase by £607,000 in 2025/26 and by £374,000 in 2026/27. It is anticipated that these costs will continue to decrease in future years.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Budgets & Finance Strategy Reports & Appendices
findings.headline: Five-year forecast identifies £400,000 funding gap in 2027/28 and £120,000 in 2028/29 to be met from general reserves.
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Finance Strategy projects explicit funding shortfalls in two consecutive years (2027/28 and 2028/29) totalling £520,000 even assuming 2.99% annual council tax increases. The council states these gaps 'can be met from the general fund reserves' but this requires reserves to absorb cumulative deficits.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether a council's spending plans are sustainable. Projected deficits in the MTFS indicate the current service model is not self-financing and depends on reserve draw-downs, which erodes the council's financial resilience.
findings.quote: Based on existing spending plans and taking account of the known variations and revenue budget pressures in future years, the projected revenue budget for the life of this year's Strategy would indicate a funding gap of £0.4 million by 2027/28 even if Council Tax is increased by 2.99% each year, and by 2028/29 there will also be a small gap of £120,000

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Budgets & Finance Strategy Reports & Appendices
findings.headline: Core funding from business rates has fallen by over £350,000 between budget-setting and forecast, showing significant income volatility.
findings.detail: The assumptions made around transitional reliefs between 2024/25 and 2025/26 have shifted materially, causing a £350,000 reduction in business rates income. This is a core funding stream and the volatility is material relative to the council's overall budget envelope.
findings.matters: Business rates are a major revenue source for local authorities. A £350k variance in one year on a council with a £15m revenue budget indicates either forecasting methodology issues or real underlying instability in the local tax base, both of concern to lenders.
findings.figures: Business rates income predicted to reduce by over £350,000 between base and revised budgets
findings.quote: The predicted level of funding from business rates has reduced by over £350,000 between the base and revised budgets. Assumptions that were made around transitional reliefs between 2024/25 and 2025/26 returns have seen the levels of income due to the council drop.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Revenue Budgets & Finance Strategy Reports & Appendices
findings.headline: 2025/26 budget now shows £56,000 shortfall despite being set as balanced, requiring draw-down from general reserves.
findings.detail: The original budget for 2025/26 was approved as balanced in February 2025. The revised budget shows a deterioration: the net revenue budget has increased to £15,282,400 with a £56,000 shortfall. This was not anticipated and will need to be funded from unallocated general reserves if not contained within year.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether budget forecasts are reliable. An in-year deterioration of this magnitude, even if small in percentage terms, suggests forecasting weakness or emerging pressures the council did not anticipate.
findings.figures: Original budget £15,050,100 (balanced); revised budget £15,282,400 (£56,000 shortfall)
findings.quote: The original General Fund revenue budget for 2025/26 set, for £15,050,100 and was a balanced budget without needing the use of general reserves to support the budget. The projected revised budget for 2025/26 is £15,282,400 which has a shortfall of £56,000 which will need to be funded from general fund reserves.

news_drafts.headline: Fareham Council anticipates a 2026/27 underspend and a contribution to reserves
news_drafts.lead:
Fareham Borough Council set its 2026/27 budget without drawing on its reserves, the money it has put aside. The latest budget monitoring report, the in-year check of spending against budget, goes to the Executive. It says any underspend will be added to general fund reserves, and that it is anticipated the year will end in underspend, "which will mean there would be a contribution to reserves". The paper adds that spending tends to rise in the later months of the year.

Two income lines are above budget to 30 September 2026. Planning applications income is almost £130k above budget, which the paper attributes mainly to an increase in major applications that bring larger fees. This is partly offset by higher employee costs. Car park income is £102k above budget, which the paper attributes to higher town centre and coastal parking levels. An underspend on business rates has also helped that service, partly offset by higher maintenance costs.

The housing revenue account (HRA), the separate account for the council's own housing, paid for by rents, shows a surplus of £4.423m transferred to the HRA reserve at 30 September. That is £76k above the £4.347m budgeted for the first six months. Income is £171k above the half-year budget, mainly from 2025/26 service charge adjustments and a Council Housebuilding Support grant rolled forward. The paper says the surplus does not yet reflect year-end corporate recharges and reserve adjustments. It says the full-year forecast outturn, the actual figures once the year has ended, is expected to be in line with budget.
